morningSummary:
Good morning. Sunday’s edition begins with the Bayelsa boat disaster, where Governor Douye Diri says 23 bodies have been recovered and 24 people rescued. The Associated Press, citing NEMA, reports 24 bodies recovered, so the figures remain inconsistent across official updates. The governor has ordered an investigation; preliminary findings point to overloading, no passenger manifest and widespread absence of life jackets. The operator reportedly fled and the boat manager is in custody for investigation. The tragedy demands transparent casualty reporting, accountability and enforceable waterway-safety rules.

Nigeria's democratic institutions face another test as INEC's preliminary voter register comes under scrutiny. Sunday PUNCH reports that AI-generated photographs and questionable entries were found, while INEC's clean-up removed 1,609,553 invalid registrations, identified 873 deceased voters and flagged 54 people across 10 states. These irregularities do not prove a coordinated plan to rig the 2027 election, but they make transparency, independent auditing and public confidence essential. Former President Goodluck Jonathan has called for an end to money politics and stronger internal party democracy. Opposition parties have also alleged billboard destruction and restrictions on campaign venues; state governments deny targeting them. Both claims and responses require evidence and fair investigation.

In Ghana, President John Mahama is urging the parliamentary Minority to support a proposed US$10 billion New Economy programme for 2027–2030, even if its success benefits the governing party. The programme's targets include agriculture, energy, mineral processing, tourism and technology. A separate poll reported by Citi Newsroom says 51 per cent of young voters surveyed were satisfied with the 24-hour Economy policy, but the summary available does not provide full methodology.

Europe faces two immediate developments. France saw a sixth weekend of demonstrations over living costs, public services, student conditions and policing; turnout estimates differ between organisers and the Interior Ministry. In Belgium, air traffic controller Skeyes says regular air traffic cannot be guaranteed from 7am to 9pm on Monday, 23 November, and airports expect major cancellations during the national strike. The UK and EU have agreed a package on food trade, carbon markets and youth mobility, while Britain and Ukraine have agreed to manufacture medium- and long-range drones in the UK.

In North America, Canadian Defence Minister David McGuinty says military cooperation with the United States continues despite reports of a classified Pentagon directive. The reported memo has not been made public and its precise scope remains unclear. President Donald Trump says he wants a permanent agreement with Iran preventing it from obtaining a nuclear weapon; this is an expressed objective, not a negotiated or accepted deal.

In Asia, a fire at an Indonesian candy factory has killed three people, with 36 workers still unaccounted for and 15 rescued. South Korea's education minister has resigned after an exam-cheating scandal involving a miniature camera and smartphone, renewing debate about AI-era assessment security. In the Middle East, UNIFIL has begun handing over some positions in southern Lebanon to the Lebanese army ahead of the peacekeeping mission's mandate ending on 31 December 2026.

At COP31 in Türkiye, negotiators have moved towards a revised climate package, but formal adoption was not confirmed in the sources reviewed for this edition. The key tests remain fossil-fuel language and finance for climate adaptation. Global technology markets are also reassessing AI valuations after the Nasdaq fell 10 per cent over the week to 20 November. In sport, Carlos Alcaraz and Alexander Zverev are scheduled to contest the ATP Finals title in Turin.

featured.title: Bayelsa boat disaster: death toll rises as governor orders investigation and safety enforcement
featured.category: Nigeria / Public Safety / Bayelsa / Water Transport
featured.summary: At least 23 bodies had been recovered and 24 survivors rescued, according to Governor Douye Diri's latest update reported by PUNCH. The Associated Press, citing NEMA, reported 24 bodies recovered. The figures differ as search operations continue. Preliminary findings point to overloading, no passenger manifest and inadequate life jackets.
featured.content:
An overloaded boat carrying mourners from Ayama to Ukubie for a burial ceremony capsized near the Oweikorogha–Otuan river junction in Southern Ijaw Local Government Area on Friday, 20 November. The tragedy has exposed serious questions about passenger safety on the Niger Delta's waterways. In an update published late on Saturday, PUNCH reported Governor Douye Diri as saying that 23 bodies had been recovered and 24 survivors rescued. The governor ordered an immediate investigation and said anyone found culpable should face prosecution. He also said preliminary findings indicated that the boat was overloaded, had no passenger manifest and that most passengers were not wearing life jackets. The state government announced plans to procure modern boats and establish a Maritime Task Force to monitor operators and enforce safety rules.

There is a discrepancy in the reported death toll: the governor's update carried by PUNCH gave 23 recovered bodies, while an Associated Press report citing NEMA said 24 bodies had been recovered. The earlier police statement had confirmed four bodies and 24 rescues. These are evolving figures from different official briefings, not a settled final casualty list. RadiantWaves is retaining the attribution rather than silently choosing one number. The police said the boat operator fled and the boat manager was taken into custody for investigation. No conclusion about criminal responsibility should be drawn before the investigation is completed.

The immediate questions are whether the vessel was licensed and seaworthy, how many people were on board, who authorised the journey, whether life jackets were available, and why enforcement failed to prevent unsafe operation. A task force and modern boats may help, but lasting prevention requires passenger manifests, routine inspections, enforceable capacity limits, functioning life-saving equipment and consequences for operators who breach safety rules.

topStories.title: INEC voter-register concerns put 2027 election credibility under scrutiny
topStories.summary: PUNCH reports that AI-generated photographs and questionable records were found in the preliminary voters' register. INEC says it removed 1,609,553 invalid registrations, identified 873 verified deceased voters and flagged 54 people across 10 states as complicit in irregularities. The discovery has not proved a coordinated plan to rig the 2027 election.
topStories.content:
A Sunday PUNCH investigation published on 22 November reports that AI-generated photographs were identified in the preliminary register of voters ahead of the 2027 general election. The report says INEC identified questionable records during the public display of the preliminary register from 9 to 15 October and later uploaded the register online on 26 October. INEC's clean-up reportedly removed 1,609,553 invalid registrations, identified 873 verified deceased voters and found 54 people across 10 states to be implicated in registration irregularities.

The concern is not simply the presence of suspicious photographs. A credible voters' register must contain genuine, eligible voters, avoid duplicate or deceased entries and protect legitimate citizens from wrongful removal. Electoral experts quoted by PUNCH argue that the register is the foundation of election credibility and have called for an independent forensic audit. The report also notes that the EU Election Observation Mission raised register-quality concerns after the 2023 election.

However, the discovery does not by itself establish that a coordinated political operation has been organised to manipulate the 2027 result. The same report quotes civil-society voices warning against reaching that conclusion without concrete evidence. INEC's national commissioner Mohammed Haruna said the commission would investigate the matter and pursue those responsible. The next test is whether the commission publishes a transparent account of the affected records, how the controls failed, what disciplinary or criminal action follows and how legitimate voters can challenge errors.

topStories.whyItMatters: Trust in the register affects every party and every eligible voter. Weak controls can damage confidence before campaigning even reaches polling day.
topStories.whatHappensNext: Watch for INEC's investigation, disclosure of findings, any prosecutions, independent audit proposals and procedures for voters to correct or challenge their details.

topStories.title: Jonathan calls for end to money politics and stronger internal party democracy
topStories.summary: Former President Goodluck Jonathan says money, patronage and ethnic considerations are weakening leadership selection and Nigeria's international reputation. He called for credible elections, internal party democracy and merit-based public appointments.
topStories.content:
Former President Goodluck Jonathan has called for reforms to Nigeria's political and leadership recruitment systems, arguing that money, patronage, ethnicity and personal connections too often outweigh competence and merit. Speaking at the Paul Alaje Colloquium in Abuja on Saturday, he said credible elections and stronger internal party democracy were essential to restoring the country's international standing.

Jonathan linked political practices to wider economic consequences, saying corruption, insecurity, abuse of public office and weak institutions undermine investor confidence and international partnerships. He also argued that Nigeria should invest more consistently in education, healthcare, agriculture, manufacturing, technology and infrastructure, while supporting creative industries and sports as instruments of cultural diplomacy.

His remarks arrive as parties prepare for the 2027 general election and debate candidate selection, coalitions and electoral credibility. They are a former president's assessment and policy argument, not an independent measurement of every party's internal processes. The challenge for all political organisations is to demonstrate transparent primaries, fair access to party structures, credible candidate selection and accountability to members and voters.

topStories.title: Opposition parties allege campaign billboard destruction; state governments deny targeting rivals
topStories.summary: Opposition parties told Sunday PUNCH that billboards were destroyed and public venues restricted in some states. The Benue government rejected claims of political intimidation and said ruling-party billboards were also vandalised.
topStories.content:
Opposition parties in several states have complained about the destruction of campaign billboards, high campaign fees and difficulties securing public venues ahead of the 2027 elections. Sunday PUNCH reports that the ADC and other opposition groups alleged that their campaign materials were being removed and that access to public facilities was being restricted.

In Benue, ADC chairman Adikwu Elias accused the state government of denying opposition parties access to public facilities and said campaign materials had been destroyed. The state Commissioner for Information, Solomon Iorpev, rejected the allegation that the government was targeting opposition groups. He said billboards belonging to the ruling party had also been vandalised and that the government was considering a task force with security agencies to identify those responsible. He urged parties seeking public facilities to follow due process.

These are competing accounts and should be investigated rather than treated as established fact. Equal access to lawful campaign spaces, protection of political property and impartial enforcement of public-space rules are essential to fair competition. Where vandalism occurs, authorities should investigate regardless of party affiliation and publish the outcome.

topStories.title: Tinubu courts South-West support in Ibadan and defends reform agenda
topStories.summary: At Saturday's Mapo Hall rally, President Bola Tinubu urged supporters to stay the course, highlighted the proposed Yutong–Leyland factory reopening and made an unnamed 'palẹmọ' remark interpreted by some outlets as a swipe at Seyi Makinde's APM.
topStories.content:
President Bola Tinubu used his visit to Ibadan on Saturday to seek South-West support for his administration and the APC's 2027 campaign. The Guardian reported that he told traditional rulers, led by the Olubadan of Ibadan, Oba Rashidi Ladoja, that the sacrifices associated with his economic reforms would lead to greater prosperity. Tinubu cited an agreement with China's Yutong to reopen the former Leyland Automobile Assembly Plant, saying the project could support vehicle assembly and employment.

At the Mapo Hall rally, he endorsed APC candidates for Oyo, Ogun and Lagos and made a remark about a group he called the 'palẹmọ' faction. Naija News reported that the comment did not name Governor Seyi Makinde or the APM, although it was interpreted as directed at Makinde's political platform. RadiantWaves distinguishes the President's words from media interpretation.

The political test for the administration is whether the promised industrial activity, employment and economic reforms produce measurable benefits for households and businesses. The opposition is entitled to challenge the record, while the government should publish project milestones, financing details, job estimates and delivery dates.

topStories.title: France sees sixth weekend of protests over living costs, public services and student conditions
topStories.summary: AFP reports that organisers estimated 150,000 participants nationwide while the Interior Ministry counted 82,500. Turnout fell from the previous week, but demonstrations continued amid concerns about prices, schools and policing.
topStories.content:
France experienced another weekend of demonstrations on Saturday, the sixth consecutive weekend of protests linked to living costs, public services and student conditions. AFP, carried by Arab News, reported that organisers estimated 150,000 participants nationwide, compared with 200,000 the previous week. The Interior Ministry counted 82,500, down from 106,000 the previous Saturday. The two figures are attributed estimates and should not be combined or presented as a single agreed count.

The movement began with high-school students demanding better learning conditions and expanded to include concerns about rising prices, public services, inequality and police conduct. In Paris, demonstrators gathered at Place de la République before marching east. AFP reported that most demonstrations were peaceful, although clashes occurred at the margins in some locations; the Interior Ministry said 144 people had been arrested by 6pm.

The protests also followed parliament's adoption of a law increasing protections for law-enforcement officers using their weapons, which critics say risks weakening accountability. The debate reflects wider pressure on the government over purchasing power, public services and policing. The scale of the protests has declined, but the underlying grievances have not disappeared.

topStories.title: Belgium warns of major flight cancellations during Monday's national strike
topStories.summary: Air traffic controller Skeyes says it cannot guarantee regular air traffic from 7am to 9pm on Monday, 23 November. Brussels Airport expects most flights to be cancelled; essential emergency flights may continue.
topStories.content:
Belgium is preparing for major disruption to air travel on Monday, 23 November, after air traffic controller Skeyes said staffing levels would not allow it to guarantee the safe handling of regular air traffic between 7am and 9pm. AFP reported that Brussels Airport expects the majority of arriving and departing flights to be cancelled. Charleroi Airport said the strike would shut down regular operations across the country's airports for the day.

The action is part of a national strike against government austerity measures and proposed savings intended to reduce Belgium's budget deficit. Skeyes said essential minimum services for emergencies and other safety-critical flights would remain available. Passengers should check directly with their airline and airport before travelling, because schedules and cancellation policies may change.

The dispute reflects broader tensions over public spending, government cost-cutting and the effect of austerity on workers and essential services.

topStories.title: Canada says military cooperation with US continues despite reported Pentagon restrictions
topStories.category: North America / Canada / Defence / US Relations
topStories.summary: Canadian Defence Minister David McGuinty said he had seen no change in military cooperation with Washington. The reported classified Pentagon directive has not been publicly examined, and its precise scope remains unclear.
topStories.content:
Canadian Defence Minister David McGuinty said on Saturday that he had seen no change in military cooperation with the United States, despite a Washington Post report about a classified Pentagon directive imposing new restrictions on defence ties. Speaking to Reuters at a security conference in Halifax, McGuinty said the two countries' militaries continued to work closely on continental defence, counter-narcotics operations and responses to threats in North American airspace.

The Washington Post report cited officials familiar with the matter, but said it had not seen the memo. The Pentagon said it was refocusing engagement with Canada around US defence priorities, while stating that the reported guidance did not affect NORAD, NATO cooperation or defence intelligence. The exact scope of any restrictions therefore remains unclear.

Canada has announced plans to raise defence spending to 5 per cent of GDP by 2035. The issue is important because Canada and the United States share integrated defence systems and a long-standing security relationship. The public record currently contains a Canadian minister's account, a media report about a classified directive and a Pentagon explanation; these should not be collapsed into a claim that cooperation has ended.

topStories.title: COP31 negotiators move towards a deal, but fossil-fuel language remains a key test
topStories.summary: Reuters reports that Australia and Türkiye presented a revised package intended to secure consensus among nearly 200 delegations. The COP president said a text had been put forward for agreement, but formal adoption had not been confirmed in the sources reviewed.
topStories.content:
Climate negotiations at COP31 in Antalya continued into Sunday after missing their scheduled Friday finish. Reuters reported that COP31 President Murat Kurum said a revised package had been presented which he believed all parties could accept. The conference was expected to reconvene on Sunday morning to consider approval.

The revised text followed criticism of an earlier draft for omitting explicit reference to ending fossil-fuel use and for failing to satisfy demands for stronger adaptation finance. Kurum said the new text addressed concerns about fossil fuels and financial support for developing countries adapting to climate change. Nearly 200 delegations have been involved in negotiations, with Australia leading the talks and Türkiye hosting the summit.

A proposal being described as close to consensus is not the same as an adopted decision. The final wording matters because countries vulnerable to floods, droughts and extreme heat are seeking predictable support, while economies dependent on fossil-fuel production and consumption are resisting language they consider too restrictive. As of the verification point for this edition, RadiantWaves had not confirmed formal adoption of the final package.

topStories.title: Factory fire in Indonesia leaves three dead and 36 workers unaccounted for
topStories.summary: Associated Press reports that a fire at a candy factory in Banten province killed three people, while 36 workers remained unaccounted for. Fifteen people were rescued, including four injured workers.
topStories.content:
A fire swept through the PT Fonusa Agung Mulia candy factory in Serang district, Banten province, on Saturday. The Associated Press reported that three people had died and 36 workers remained unaccounted for as rescue teams searched the damaged facility. Fifteen people were rescued alive, including four injured workers. The factory produces Milkita, a milk-based candy and snack brand.

Indonesia's National Search and Rescue Agency said search operations were continuing. The fire was still burning in parts of the facility more than 12 hours after it began, according to local rescue officials. The cause of the fire had not been established in the reporting reviewed for this edition.

The immediate priority is locating missing workers and identifying the dead and injured. A later investigation will need to establish how the fire started, whether emergency exits and alarms were adequate, how quickly workers were evacuated and whether workplace fire-safety standards were followed.

topStories.title: Ghana's $10bn New Economy programme becomes a test of cross-party economic cooperation
topStories.summary: President John Mahama has urged the parliamentary Minority to support a $10bn economic transformation programme for 2027–2030, arguing that its success should matter more than which party benefits politically.
topStories.content:
Ghanaian President John Dramani Mahama has urged the parliamentary Minority to support the government's proposed $10 billion New Economy programme, saying its success would benefit the country even if it helped keep the governing National Democratic Congress in power. Citi Newsroom reported the appeal on 21 November.

The programme was outlined in Ghana's 2027 budget and is intended to support agriculture, energy infrastructure, critical minerals, tourism, textiles, pharmaceuticals and the technology economy. The Ghana News Agency reported that the government plans a US$10 billion investment framework between 2027 and 2030, with GH¢30 billion earmarked for the programme in 2027. The programme includes proposed investment in local food production, electricity generation and transmission, solar power, battery storage and value-added mineral processing.

The government's targets are ambitious and should be assessed against the final budget, financing sources, procurement transparency, implementation capacity and measurable jobs and productivity. Cross-party support does not remove the need for parliamentary scrutiny; it makes scrutiny and transparent reporting even more important.

topStories.title: Trump says he wants a permanent agreement preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon
topStories.category: World / United States / Iran / Diplomacy / Nuclear Security
topStories.summary: US President Donald Trump said he intends to secure a permanent deal preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon. The statement describes his objective; it is not evidence that a new agreement has been negotiated or accepted by Tehran.
topStories.content:
US President Donald Trump has said he intends to secure a permanent agreement with Iran that would prevent Tehran from obtaining a nuclear weapon and bind future US administrations. Anadolu's Sunday morning briefing reported the remarks made on Saturday. Trump argued that the agreement should not be reversible by a future president.

The statement sets out the US President's desired outcome, but no completed agreement was announced in the report. Any durable nuclear arrangement would require negotiations over verification, sanctions, enrichment limits, monitoring, enforcement and the political commitments of both sides. Iran's position and response must be reported separately; a US declaration of intent does not amount to Iranian acceptance.

The issue carries implications for regional security, energy markets and diplomacy across the Gulf. A credible agreement would need clear verification mechanisms and a process for addressing disputes, rather than relying solely on political assurances.

worldNews.content:
UNIFIL has begun handing over some of its positions in southern Lebanon to the Lebanese army, mission chief Diodato Abagnara said on Saturday, according to Lebanon's National News Agency as reported by Anadolu. He warned against a security vacuum after the peacekeeping mission ends and said monitoring and reporting violations, humanitarian assistance and civilian protection remain important.

The UN Security Council's Resolution 2790 (2025) extended UNIFIL's mandate for a final time until 31 December 2026 and directed an orderly drawdown and withdrawal beginning at the end of the year, to be completed within one year. UNIFIL has operated in southern Lebanon since 1978, with its mandate expanded after the 2006 conflict.

The handover is not simply an administrative transfer. Southern Lebanon remains affected by conflict and violations of the cessation-of-hostilities arrangement. The transition will depend on the Lebanese state's ability to provide security, the support available to its armed forces and whether a replacement international monitoring arrangement is agreed.

worldNews.content:
South Korea's education minister Choi Kyo-jin resigned on Sunday, taking responsibility for failures to prevent cheating involving artificial intelligence and covert technology around high-stakes examinations, according to reporting published by the Times of India. The controversy followed a case in which the top scorer in a national tax-accountant examination admitted using a miniature camera and smartphone to obtain a near-perfect score.

The scandal has intensified concern about exam security ahead of the highly competitive Suneung university entrance test. The presidential office said President Lee Jae Myung accepted the minister's resignation. The episode illustrates how small electronic devices and AI tools can challenge traditional assessment systems, particularly where a single examination can strongly influence educational and career prospects.

The case also raises questions about whether schools and examination authorities can strengthen monitoring without undermining privacy, fairness or equal access. The resignation is a political consequence; it does not by itself resolve the broader problem of detecting technology-assisted cheating.

electionWatch.title: Federal High Court rejects Atiku and ADC bid to amend Tinubu eligibility case
electionWatch.summary: Justice Inyang Ekwo refused the proposed amendments to Atiku Abubakar and the ADC's pre-election suit, but did not decide whether the NYSC discharge certificate at the centre of the case is genuine.
electionWatch.content:
Atiku Abubakar and the African Democratic Congress filed their suit against President Bola Tinubu, the All Progressives Congress and INEC on 14 August. They allege that the APC submitted a forged National Youth Service Corps discharge certificate in support of Tinubu's nomination, with the document bearing the name “Tinubu Bola Adekunle”. Tinubu and the APC deny submitting a forged certificate and say the NYSC has not denied issuing the discharge certificate.

On 20 November, Justice Inyang Ekwo rejected the plaintiffs' application to amend the case, ruling that the proposed changes would introduce fresh facts after the Constitution's 14-day limit for pre-election matters had expired. The judge directed the parties to proceed on the original filings. This is a procedural ruling: it is not a finding that the certificate is forged, and it is not a final judgment on Tinubu's eligibility.
electionWatch.imageAlt: File portrait of former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar
electionWatch.imageNote: RadiantWaves repository portrait; not a photograph of the court hearing.
electionWatch.source: Premium Times, 20–21 November 2026; Tinubu and APC's denial reported in the court coverage
electionWatch.whyItMatters: The distinction between a procedural ruling and a decision on the evidence is essential to fair reporting on presidential eligibility and the rule of law.
electionWatch.whatHappensNext: The substantive suit remains before the Federal High Court. The next substantive hearing and any further applications will determine how the original evidence is tested.
electionWatch.label: ADC / TINUBU ELIGIBILITY

electionWatch.title: Court orders ADC to restore Omar Suleiman as Adamawa governorship candidate
electionWatch.summary: The Federal High Court ordered INEC to recognise Omar Suleiman as the ADC's Adamawa candidate after finding no valid basis for replacing the primary winner with Tukur Ribadu.
electionWatch.content:
Justice Obiora Egwuatu ordered the ADC to forward Omar Suleiman's details to INEC and directed the commission not to recognise or publish Tukur Ribadu as the party's Adamawa governorship candidate. Suleiman had won the party primary in May, polling 143,216 votes across the state's 21 local government areas, according to the court report. Ribadu finished second with 56,801.

The judge found no evidence that Ribadu had successfully challenged the primary result through a properly constituted party appeal committee. The ADC and Ribadu argued that an appeal process had taken place, but affidavits from the primary committee's chairman and secretary said no such committee had been constituted. The order concerns the Adamawa governorship nomination; it is separate from the national ADC leadership appeal involving David Mark.
electionWatch.imageNote: No verified portrait of Omar Suleiman or photograph of the judgment is available in the repository.
electionWatch.whyItMatters: The ruling is a reminder that internal party primaries and nomination procedures are subject to legal scrutiny, including when party executives later change a result.
electionWatch.whatHappensNext: Watch for any appeal or further INEC action. The report reviewed for this edition records the Federal High Court order but does not establish whether an appeal has since been filed.
electionWatch.label: ADC / ADAMAWA NOMINATION

electionWatch.title: INEC awaits Court of Appeal as rival ADC factions dispute David Mark leadership
electionWatch.category: Nigeria / Politics / ADC / Electoral Commission / Judiciary
electionWatch.summary: INEC says it has been served notice of the appeal against the judgment that nullified David Mark's ADC leadership; the Nafiu Bala Gombe faction says the existing order should be enforced immediately.
electionWatch.content:
The Federal High Court judgment of 5 November nullified the Mark-led caretaker leadership and set aside actions taken under it. The Mark-led faction has filed an appeal and sought a stay of execution. INEC National Commissioner Mohammed Haruna told PUNCH that the commission had received notice of the appeal and would await the Court of Appeal's decision before determining its next step.

The rival faction led by Nafiu Bala Gombe argues that the judgment remains valid and binding because no superior court has stayed or set it aside. It wants INEC to recognise its leadership and remove Mark and former Interior Minister Rauf Aregbesola from the commission's records. The two sides therefore disagree both on the practical effect of the trial court's order and on what INEC should do while the appeal is pending. The appellate court has not yet delivered a final decision in the reports reviewed.
electionWatch.imageAlt: Repository image associated with Atiku Abubakar and David Mark
electionWatch.imageNote: Existing RadiantWaves image; illustrative of the party dispute, not a photograph of the appeal hearing.
electionWatch.whyItMatters: The dispute affects the authority to manage party records and nominations ahead of the 2027 election. It must be reported as an active legal contest, not as a settled political outcome.
electionWatch.whatHappensNext: The Court of Appeal must determine the appeal and any stay application. Until then, INEC's stated position is to await the appellate outcome, while the rival faction continues to demand immediate compliance with the trial judgment.
electionWatch.label: ADC / DAVID MARK APPEAL

electionWatch.title: Opposition coalition moves Abuja summit to 30 November
electionWatch.category: Nigeria / Politics / Opposition / ADC / APM / NDC / PDP / Elections
electionWatch.summary: The Coalition for Democracy has postponed its second summit from 23 to 30 November and says member parties will pause campaign activities nationwide for the day.
electionWatch.content:
The Coalition for Democracy moved its second summit after member parties said campaign schedules could prevent presidential candidates, national chairmen and party leaders from attending. The committee's statement, signed by Salihu Moh. Lukman, says the gathering is intended to finalise and sign a common agreement ahead of the 16 January 2027 presidential election.

The coalition includes the ADC, Allied Peoples Movement, Nigeria Democratic Congress, a faction of the PDP, Peoples Redemption Party and Social Democratic Party. Organisers say participating parties have agreed to suspend campaigns nationwide on 30 November so leaders can attend. The announcement is evidence of coordination, but it is not yet proof that the parties have agreed on one presidential candidate or resolved their internal differences.
electionWatch.imageAlt: File portrait of Atiku Abubakar from the RadiantWaves image library
electionWatch.imageNote: One of the repository's separate Atiku photographs; used as an opposition-politics illustration, not a photograph of the summit.
electionWatch.whyItMatters: Opposition cooperation could widen voter choice, but its credibility will depend on transparent decision-making, a clear programme and respect for each party's internal democratic processes.
electionWatch.whatHappensNext: The key test is whether the 30 November meeting produces a signed agreement, an accountable structure and a clear process for resolving candidate and policy differences.
electionWatch.label: OPPOSITION COALITION

electionWatch.title: Peter Obi sets 10,000MW electricity target and makes health and education pledges
electionWatch.summary: At an Onitsha town hall, Peter Obi pledged 10,000 megawatts of electricity, 10,000 primary healthcare centres and 40,000 primary-school blocks if elected.
electionWatch.content:
Peter Obi, presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress, outlined the targets during a homecoming and town-hall engagement in Onitsha. He said his administration would aim to generate, transmit and distribute at least 10,000 megawatts of electricity, build 10,000 primary healthcare centres and provide 40,000 primary-school blocks.

These are campaign commitments, not funded projects or completed government programmes. The published report did not provide a full costed plan, a construction timetable, a staffing model for the proposed health centres or a detailed financing strategy. Obi also urged supporters to remain at polling units until votes are counted and results transmitted. Voters should be able to compare these promises with budgets, delivery milestones and the candidate's record in public office.
electionWatch.imageNote: RadiantWaves repository portrait; not a photograph of the Onitsha town hall.
electionWatch.whyItMatters: Large infrastructure pledges are meaningful only when voters can see the costs, delivery timetable, staffing needs and measurable outcomes.
electionWatch.whatHappensNext: The NDC should publish costings, funding assumptions, timelines and state-by-state implementation targets so the public can test the proposal.
electionWatch.label: NDC / PETER OBI POLICY

electionWatch.title: Tinubu's Ibadan rally remark draws attention to Seyi Makinde's APM presidential bid
electionWatch.summary: President Tinubu referred to a 'palẹmọ' group at the Ibadan rally without naming Seyi Makinde or the APM; PUNCH and other outlets interpreted the remark as a swipe at the governor's presidential bid.
electionWatch.content:
President Bola Tinubu addressed an APC campaign rally at Mapo Hall in Ibadan on Saturday and urged Oyo voters to support the ruling party. He referred to an unnamed group or faction as the 'palẹmọ' group and said its members were waiting in vain. The President did not name Governor Seyi Makinde or the Allied Peoples Movement in the quoted remark.

Makinde is seeking the presidency under the APM platform. The political context makes the interpretation understandable, but a newsroom should distinguish the words actually spoken from the identity attributed to the target by commentators or reporters. The exchange is part of a competitive campaign; it does not alter the legal status of any candidate or party.
electionWatch.imageAlt: File portrait of Oyo State Governor Seyi Makinde
electionWatch.imageNote: RadiantWaves repository portrait; not a photograph of the Ibadan rally.
electionWatch.whyItMatters: The language of a campaign matters, but accuracy requires not attributing an unnamed remark to a person unless the speaker identifies them or the evidence establishes the target.
electionWatch.whatHappensNext: Watch for a direct response from Makinde or the APM and for any further campaign statements that clarify the exchange.
electionWatch.label: APM / MAKINDE CAMPAIGN

articles.title: Bayelsa boat disaster: death toll rises as governor orders investigation and safety enforcement
articles.category: Nigeria / Public Safety / Bayelsa / Water Transport
articles.summary: At least 23 bodies had been recovered and 24 survivors rescued, according to Governor Douye Diri's latest update reported by PUNCH. The Associated Press, citing NEMA, reported 24 bodies recovered. The figures differ as search operations continue. Preliminary findings point to overloading, no passenger manifest and inadequate life jackets.
articles.content:
An overloaded boat carrying mourners from Ayama to Ukubie for a burial ceremony capsized near the Oweikorogha–Otuan river junction in Southern Ijaw Local Government Area on Friday, 20 November. The tragedy has exposed serious questions about passenger safety on the Niger Delta's waterways. In an update published late on Saturday, PUNCH reported Governor Douye Diri as saying that 23 bodies had been recovered and 24 survivors rescued. The governor ordered an immediate investigation and said anyone found culpable should face prosecution. He also said preliminary findings indicated that the boat was overloaded, had no passenger manifest and that most passengers were not wearing life jackets. The state government announced plans to procure modern boats and establish a Maritime Task Force to monitor operators and enforce safety rules.

There is a discrepancy in the reported death toll: the governor's update carried by PUNCH gave 23 recovered bodies, while an Associated Press report citing NEMA said 24 bodies had been recovered. The earlier police statement had confirmed four bodies and 24 rescues. These are evolving figures from different official briefings, not a settled final casualty list. RadiantWaves is retaining the attribution rather than silently choosing one number. The police said the boat operator fled and the boat manager was taken into custody for investigation. No conclusion about criminal responsibility should be drawn before the investigation is completed.

The immediate questions are whether the vessel was licensed and seaworthy, how many people were on board, who authorised the journey, whether life jackets were available, and why enforcement failed to prevent unsafe operation. A task force and modern boats may help, but lasting prevention requires passenger manifests, routine inspections, enforceable capacity limits, functioning life-saving equipment and consequences for operators who breach safety rules.

articles.source: PUNCH, 21 November 2026; Bayelsa State Governor's statement; Associated Press, 22 November 2026; NEMA and Bayelsa Police statements as reported
articles.whyItMatters: Waterway safety is a public responsibility. Families need transparent casualty information, an independent investigation and practical safeguards before the next journey.
articles.whatHappensNext: Track the official casualty update, investigation findings, any charges, the status of the boat manager, the promised Maritime Task Force and procurement of safer vessels.

articles.title: INEC voter-register concerns put 2027 election credibility under scrutiny
articles.summary: PUNCH reports that AI-generated photographs and questionable records were found in the preliminary voters' register. INEC says it removed 1,609,553 invalid registrations, identified 873 verified deceased voters and flagged 54 people across 10 states as complicit in irregularities. The discovery has not proved a coordinated plan to rig the 2027 election.
articles.content:
A Sunday PUNCH investigation published on 22 November reports that AI-generated photographs were identified in the preliminary register of voters ahead of the 2027 general election. The report says INEC identified questionable records during the public display of the preliminary register from 9 to 15 October and later uploaded the register online on 26 October. INEC's clean-up reportedly removed 1,609,553 invalid registrations, identified 873 verified deceased voters and found 54 people across 10 states to be implicated in registration irregularities.

The concern is not simply the presence of suspicious photographs. A credible voters' register must contain genuine, eligible voters, avoid duplicate or deceased entries and protect legitimate citizens from wrongful removal. Electoral experts quoted by PUNCH argue that the register is the foundation of election credibility and have called for an independent forensic audit. The report also notes that the EU Election Observation Mission raised register-quality concerns after the 2023 election.

However, the discovery does not by itself establish that a coordinated political operation has been organised to manipulate the 2027 result. The same report quotes civil-society voices warning against reaching that conclusion without concrete evidence. INEC's national commissioner Mohammed Haruna said the commission would investigate the matter and pursue those responsible. The next test is whether the commission publishes a transparent account of the affected records, how the controls failed, what disciplinary or criminal action follows and how legitimate voters can challenge errors.

articles.source: PUNCH, 22 November 2026; INEC statements and civil-society comments reported by Sunday PUNCH
articles.whyItMatters: Trust in the register affects every party and every eligible voter. Weak controls can damage confidence before campaigning even reaches polling day.
articles.whatHappensNext: Watch for INEC's investigation, disclosure of findings, any prosecutions, independent audit proposals and procedures for voters to correct or challenge their details.
articles.label: INEC / VOTER REGISTER

articles.title: Jonathan calls for end to money politics and stronger internal party democracy
articles.summary: Former President Goodluck Jonathan says money, patronage and ethnic considerations are weakening leadership selection and Nigeria's international reputation. He called for credible elections, internal party democracy and merit-based public appointments.
articles.content:
Former President Goodluck Jonathan has called for reforms to Nigeria's political and leadership recruitment systems, arguing that money, patronage, ethnicity and personal connections too often outweigh competence and merit. Speaking at the Paul Alaje Colloquium in Abuja on Saturday, he said credible elections and stronger internal party democracy were essential to restoring the country's international standing.

Jonathan linked political practices to wider economic consequences, saying corruption, insecurity, abuse of public office and weak institutions undermine investor confidence and international partnerships. He also argued that Nigeria should invest more consistently in education, healthcare, agriculture, manufacturing, technology and infrastructure, while supporting creative industries and sports as instruments of cultural diplomacy.

His remarks arrive as parties prepare for the 2027 general election and debate candidate selection, coalitions and electoral credibility. They are a former president's assessment and policy argument, not an independent measurement of every party's internal processes. The challenge for all political organisations is to demonstrate transparent primaries, fair access to party structures, credible candidate selection and accountability to members and voters.

articles.whatHappensNext: Look for concrete party reforms, transparent primary rules, published campaign-finance safeguards and credible enforcement against vote-buying.

articles.title: Opposition parties allege campaign billboard destruction; state governments deny targeting rivals
articles.summary: Opposition parties told Sunday PUNCH that billboards were destroyed and public venues restricted in some states. The Benue government rejected claims of political intimidation and said ruling-party billboards were also vandalised.
articles.content:
Opposition parties in several states have complained about the destruction of campaign billboards, high campaign fees and difficulties securing public venues ahead of the 2027 elections. Sunday PUNCH reports that the ADC and other opposition groups alleged that their campaign materials were being removed and that access to public facilities was being restricted.

In Benue, ADC chairman Adikwu Elias accused the state government of denying opposition parties access to public facilities and said campaign materials had been destroyed. The state Commissioner for Information, Solomon Iorpev, rejected the allegation that the government was targeting opposition groups. He said billboards belonging to the ruling party had also been vandalised and that the government was considering a task force with security agencies to identify those responsible. He urged parties seeking public facilities to follow due process.

These are competing accounts and should be investigated rather than treated as established fact. Equal access to lawful campaign spaces, protection of political property and impartial enforcement of public-space rules are essential to fair competition. Where vandalism occurs, authorities should investigate regardless of party affiliation and publish the outcome.

articles.source: Sunday PUNCH, 22 November 2026; statements by ADC representatives and Benue State Government
articles.whyItMatters: Political competition is not fair if parties cannot campaign peacefully and lawfully. Allegations of intimidation require evidence and a response from the authorities concerned.
articles.whatHappensNext: Seek police records, local government venue policies, documented complaints and outcomes of any investigations into billboard destruction.

articles.title: Tinubu courts South-West support in Ibadan and defends reform agenda
articles.summary: At Saturday's Mapo Hall rally, President Bola Tinubu urged supporters to stay the course, highlighted the proposed Yutong–Leyland factory reopening and made an unnamed 'palẹmọ' remark interpreted by some outlets as a swipe at Seyi Makinde's APM.
articles.content:
President Bola Tinubu used his visit to Ibadan on Saturday to seek South-West support for his administration and the APC's 2027 campaign. The Guardian reported that he told traditional rulers, led by the Olubadan of Ibadan, Oba Rashidi Ladoja, that the sacrifices associated with his economic reforms would lead to greater prosperity. Tinubu cited an agreement with China's Yutong to reopen the former Leyland Automobile Assembly Plant, saying the project could support vehicle assembly and employment.

At the Mapo Hall rally, he endorsed APC candidates for Oyo, Ogun and Lagos and made a remark about a group he called the 'palẹmọ' faction. Naija News reported that the comment did not name Governor Seyi Makinde or the APM, although it was interpreted as directed at Makinde's political platform. In an update published late on Saturday, PUNCH reported Governor Douye Diri as saying that 23 bodies had been recovered and 24 survivors rescued. UNIFIL has operated in southern Lebanon since 1978, with its mandate expanded after the 2006 conflict.

The handover is not simply an administrative transfer. Southern Lebanon remains affected by conflict and violations of the cessation-of-hostilities arrangement. The move reflected concerns about high valuations, the scale of data-centre investment, future earnings and the concentration of investor expectations around artificial intelligence. Some market participants described it as a repricing after a period of strong gains, while others questioned whether expected revenue can justify the spending commitments. Those are market interpretations, not settled forecasts. The next trading sessions and company results will provide more evidence.

The wider lesson is that enthusiasm for a transformative technology can coexist with substantial financial risk. Investors, pension funds and businesses are exposed when valuations assume rapid growth before the returns are established.

technologyNews.title: INEC voter-register concerns put 2027 election credibility under scrutiny
technologyNews.summary: PUNCH reports that AI-generated photographs and questionable records were found in the preliminary voters' register. INEC says it removed 1,609,553 invalid registrations, identified 873 verified deceased voters and flagged 54 people across 10 states as complicit in irregularities. The discovery has not proved a coordinated plan to rig the 2027 election.
technologyNews.content:
A Sunday PUNCH investigation published on 22 November reports that AI-generated photographs were identified in the preliminary register of voters ahead of the 2027 general election. The report says INEC identified questionable records during the public display of the preliminary register from 9 to 15 October and later uploaded the register online on 26 October. INEC's clean-up reportedly removed 1,609,553 invalid registrations, identified 873 verified deceased voters and found 54 people across 10 states to be implicated in registration irregularities.

The concern is not simply the presence of suspicious photographs. A credible voters' register must contain genuine, eligible voters, avoid duplicate or deceased entries and protect legitimate citizens from wrongful removal. Electoral experts quoted by PUNCH argue that the register is the foundation of election credibility and have called for an independent forensic audit. The report also notes that the EU Election Observation Mission raised register-quality concerns after the 2023 election.

However, the discovery does not by itself establish that a coordinated political operation has been organised to manipulate the 2027 result. The same report quotes civil-society voices warning against reaching that conclusion without concrete evidence. INEC's national commissioner Mohammed Haruna said the commission would investigate the matter and pursue those responsible. The next test is whether the commission publishes a transparent account of the affected records, how the controls failed, what disciplinary or criminal action follows and how legitimate voters can challenge errors.

editorial.title: A credible 2027 election begins with a trustworthy register and a level playing field
editorial.imageNote: No verified image required for this editorial.
editorial.summary: The discovery of questionable voter records and complaints about campaign access should trigger transparent investigations, not premature conclusions or partisan denial.
editorial.content:
The credibility of an election is built long before ballot papers are counted. It begins with a voter register that citizens can trust, political parties that can organise freely and institutions that apply the rules impartially. Reports that AI-generated photographs and questionable entries appeared in the preliminary voters' register deserve serious attention. INEC says it has removed more than 1.6 million invalid registrations and identified people implicated in irregularities. That is a significant clean-up, but it is not the end of the matter. The commission must explain how the weaknesses occurred, identify those responsible and demonstrate that eligible voters have not been wrongly excluded.

At the same time, opposition parties have alleged that campaign billboards were destroyed and access to public venues restricted in some states. The governments concerned have rejected claims of deliberate intimidation and, in Benue, said ruling-party billboards were also vandalised. These allegations require evidence, independent investigation and responses from the authorities. No party should be above scrutiny, and no party should be denied lawful political participation.

Former President Goodluck Jonathan's warning about money politics and weak internal party democracy adds another dimension. Voters need genuine choices, transparent candidate selection and political parties that respect their own rules. The same standard applies to the governing party and every opposition platform.

RadiantWaves calls for an independent audit of the voter register, transparent publication of INEC's findings, equal access to lawful campaign facilities and prompt investigation of political violence and vandalism. A credible election is not a favour granted by those in power. It is a right owed to every eligible voter.
editorial.source: RadiantWaves Editorial Desk; PUNCH, 22 November 2026; INEC statements reported by Sunday PUNCH

analysis.title: Bayelsa boat disaster: a tragedy that exposes gaps in waterway safety enforcement
analysis.imageNote: No verified event image in the repository; do not use an unrelated boat photograph.
analysis.summary: The evolving casualty reports point to a wider failure of safety systems: vessel capacity, manifests, life jackets, inspections and enforcement.
analysis.content:
An overloaded boat carrying mourners from Ayama to Ukubie for a burial ceremony capsized near the Oweikorogha–Otuan river junction in Southern Ijaw Local Government Area on Friday, 20 November. The tragedy has exposed serious questions about passenger safety on the Niger Delta's waterways. In an update published late on Saturday, PUNCH reported Governor Douye Diri as saying that 23 bodies had been recovered and 24 survivors rescued. The governor ordered an immediate investigation and said anyone found culpable should face prosecution. He also said preliminary findings indicated that the boat was overloaded, had no passenger manifest and that most passengers were not wearing life jackets. The state government announced plans to procure modern boats and establish a Maritime Task Force to monitor operators and enforce safety rules.

There is a discrepancy in the reported death toll: the governor's update carried by PUNCH gave 23 recovered bodies, while an Associated Press report citing NEMA said 24 bodies had been recovered. The earlier police statement had confirmed four bodies and 24 rescues. These are evolving figures from different official briefings, not a settled final casualty list. RadiantWaves is retaining the attribution rather than silently choosing one number. The police said the boat operator fled and the boat manager was taken into custody for investigation. No conclusion about criminal responsibility should be drawn before the investigation is completed.

The immediate questions are whether the vessel was licensed and seaworthy, how many people were on board, who authorised the journey, whether life jackets were available, and why enforcement failed to prevent unsafe operation. A task force and modern boats may help, but lasting prevention requires passenger manifests, routine inspections, enforceable capacity limits, functioning life-saving equipment and consequences for operators who breach safety rules.

The policy response must go beyond replacing wooden boats. A safer system requires routine vessel inspection, registration, passenger manifests, enforceable capacity limits, compulsory life jackets, trained operators, emergency communications and transparent prosecution where negligence is proved. Government procurement announcements should be accompanied by budgets, delivery schedules and public reporting. The investigation should also examine the regulatory agencies responsible for monitoring commercial passenger transport on the waterways.
analysis.source: PUNCH, 21 November 2026; Bayelsa State Governor's statement; Associated Press, 22 November 2026; NEMA and Bayelsa Police statements as reported

publicInterestFeature.content:
INEC has published polling units selected for its nationwide mock accreditation exercise scheduled for 28 November. The commission says the exercise will test accreditation, result uploads and whether staff and equipment can reach polling units on time. It has explained that presiding officers will photograph completed Form EC8A sheets using BVAS and enter figures electronically, after which the system compares the two records and flags discrepancies. INEC says the paper form remains the official polling-unit record.

Atiku and the ADC have asked for independent technical scrutiny and clearer procedures for resolving flagged results. That request is a party demand, not proof that the system is defective. Public confidence will depend on transparent documentation, observer access, audit trails, clear correction procedures and equal information for all parties.

middaySummary: Today's main developments included the Federal High Court's refusal to let Atiku Abubakar and the ADC amend their Tinubu eligibility suit, a separate order restoring Omar Suleiman as the ADC's Adamawa candidate, and INEC's decision to await the Court of Appeal in the national leadership dispute involving David Mark. The Coalition for Democracy has moved its summit to 30 November. Outside Nigeria, France's protests continued with lower turnout, the UK and EU agreed a new cooperation package, and COP31 negotiations ran beyond their scheduled close.
eveningSummary:
At Mapo Hall in Ibadan, President Bola Tinubu renewed his assurance that electricity supply would improve and announced an agreement with China's Yutong to reopen the old Leyland factory. The rally was subdued following the Bayelsa boat tragedy; reports describe a large APC gathering, but turnout at a party rally is not a measure of statewide public opinion. The speech has revived scrutiny of Tinubu's 2023 electricity pledge. Its fuller wording, as reproduced by the APC campaign council, included a qualification that he could give Nigerians adequate reasons if he failed to deliver before seeking a second term. NERC's Q2 2026 report recorded average hourly generation of 4,022.40 MWh/h, while The Guardian, citing NISO, reported about 3,180 MW on the evening of 18 November. The government points to reforms, metering and debt repayment; the public-interest question is whether these measures have translated into reliable supply and accurate billing for households and businesses. The viral newspaper-front-page collage supplied to RadiantWaves has not been authenticated because it contains no dates, bylines or original links.

Good evening. Nigeria's opposition politics is again under legal scrutiny, but three separate court matters must not be confused. The Federal High Court refused Atiku Abubakar and the ADC permission to amend their challenge to President Bola Tinubu's 2027 eligibility; the substantive case remains pending and the judge did not rule on the authenticity of the NYSC certificate. In a separate Adamawa case, another judge ordered the ADC to restore Omar Suleiman as its governorship candidate. The national leadership dispute involving David Mark is before the Court of Appeal, with INEC saying it will await the appellate outcome while the rival faction demands immediate enforcement of the trial judgment.

The Coalition for Democracy has moved its second summit to 30 November and says participating parties—including the ADC, APM, NDC, a PDP faction, PRP and SDP—will pause campaign activity for the day. The meeting is expected to finalise a common agreement, but no common presidential candidate has been announced. Peter Obi has set campaign targets of 10,000 megawatts of electricity, 10,000 primary healthcare centres and 40,000 primary-school blocks; the public still needs costings and a delivery timetable. In Ibadan, President Tinubu made an unnamed 'palẹmọ' remark that some outlets interpreted as a swipe at Seyi Makinde's APM bid, although the President did not name him.

Nigeria also faces urgent public-safety and governance questions. Gombe State says three people died and 13 were injured in Lawanti after a confrontation involving residents and alleged military personnel; residents accuse Air Force personnel of opening fire, but the circumstances remain subject to official verification and the governor has ordered an impartial probe. In Bayelsa, police confirmed four deaths—including two children—and 24 rescues after a boat carrying mourners capsized. Customs has paused training for 3,852 recruits while it consults the Federal Character Commission over disputed exclusions and invitations.

In Africa, coalition negotiations in South Africa could keep the DA outside governing arrangements in Johannesburg, Tshwane and Ekurhuleni despite its position as the largest single party in each metro. Guinea has sentenced 224 people in an illegal gold-mining crackdown, while Ethiopia and Sudan continue to trade accusations about support for armed groups; the latter claims have not been independently verified and both governments deny wrongdoing.

In Europe, French prosecutors are investigating suspected leaks of confidential information to Marine Le Pen's National Rally, but no one had been formally charged in the reports reviewed. Separate protests over living costs and student rights drew lower turnout on Saturday, with official and organisers' estimates differing. The UK and EU have agreed a package on food trade, carbon markets and youth mobility; the youth scheme is for eligible UK and EU citizens aged 18–31 and is not due to begin before 2030. In Ukraine, local officials say a Russian strike on Kryvyi Rih killed two people and wounded 60.

In North America, President Donald Trump's new order requires federal contractors to coordinate with the White House before responding to certain congressional inquiries, raising a fresh test of executive privilege and legislative oversight. In Canada, Mark Carney's effort to diversify trade through closer engagement with China has prompted a warning from Taiwan that dependence can create political leverage; that warning is a policy assessment, not proof of coercion in Canada.

In Asia, Australia and China have agreed to establish a bilateral dialogue on AI safety, governance and applications while continuing to manage wider strategic differences. Japan and India have signed a letter of intent that would allow Japanese forces to conduct live-fire training at Indian ranges, including surface-to-ship missile exercises, once arrangements are implemented.

In the Middle East, Reuters reports that an Israeli strike hit a Gaza vehicle carrying food and killed three people according to the Gaza Health Ministry. Witnesses saw World Central Kitchen branding, but WCK said the vehicle was not affiliated with it; Israel said it was targeting Islamic Jihad, a claim Reuters could not independently verify. UKMTO has reported two tanker incidents near Oman's Khasab, but responsibility remains unknown. In Iraq, a fire at the Hartha power station killed four and injured 35, prompting an official investigation.

Business and technology markets remain volatile. The Nasdaq fell 5.3% on Friday and 10% for the week as investors reassessed AI valuations and spending, while oil benchmarks were on track for a third weekly decline on strong Middle East exports. COP31 negotiations in Antalya continued beyond the scheduled close, with countries divided over fossil-fuel language and climate-adaptation finance. As of this edition's 19:39 CET verification point, no final cover decision had been confirmed.
